share_verdict: Sesame and jaggery, once. Besan and syrup, now.

source.text: Sweet balls of jaggery, sesame and coconut — laḍḍukā — are an old class of festival sweet; the Mānasollāsa (12th CE) describes modaka-type sweets among festival foods, though the rolled ball and the steamed dumpling are distinct lines.
source.century: Pre-12th CE, with the Mānasollāsa description 12th CE

ingredients.name: jaggery
ingredients.function: the sweetener and the binder; melted, it sets the ball as it cools

ingredients.name: sesame
ingredients.function: fat, calcium and the toasty flavour; til-guḍ is one of the oldest sweet pairings on the subcontinent

ingredients.name: ghee
ingredients.function: carries the aromatics and stops the mix seizing

method_reconstructed: Roast the sesame until it pops.
Melt the jaggery with a splash of water to a soft-ball consistency.
Stir in coconut, sesame and ghee off the flame.
Add crushed cardamom and roll into balls while warm.
contested_points: The rolled sweet ball recorded here and the steamed modak are two lines of the old word modaka; the steamed dumpling now has its own record.
The besan (gram flour) laddu that most people picture is a later development and depends on finely milled gram flour.

changed.to: refined white sugar, and in commercial sweets, sugar syrup
changed.driver: industrial refining made white sugar cheaper and more uniform than jaggery, and it became the aspirational choice

changed.to: finely milled besan and refined flour
changed.driver: roller and plate milling; a fine flour gives the smooth commercial texture people now expect

ingredients: 1 cup grated jaggery, or palm jaggery
steps: Dry-roast the sesame until it pops, then set aside.
Melt the jaggery with two tablespoons of water. Cook until a drop set in cold water forms a soft ball.
Off the heat, stir in coconut, sesame and ghee.
Add cardamom. Roll while warm, it will not roll once cold.
Darker, coarser and less sweet than a shop laddu, and it tastes of sesame.

verification.note: Seed record, split from the former combined modaka/laddu entry: the steamed modak is now a separate record. Composite description; not yet checked against a printed edition, so no verse number or page is claimed.
